# Introduction to Thermodynamics {#sec-ch1}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- Define thermodynamics and explain its real-world applications.
- Explain important thermodynamic terms such as **system**, **state**,
  **property**, **temperature** and **pressure**.
- Use the **equation of state** to solve ideal-gas problems.
:::

## Definition

Thermodynamics is the study of the effects of energy transfer via **heat** and
**work** on a system.

![](figures/img/thermo-heat-work.png){width=34%}

Thermodynamics has its roots in the study of engines that convert heat
(*thermo*) into movement (*dynamics*).

![](figures/img/steam-locomotive.png){width=26%}

## Applications

All applications in nature involve some interaction between energy and matter;
it is therefore hard to imagine an area that does not relate to thermodynamics
in some way.

![Refrigerators, power plants, car engines, jet engines and the human body are all thermodynamic systems.](figures/img/applications.png){width=72%}

## Macroscopic description

The behaviour of individual molecules is studied in **statistical** or
**microscopic** thermodynamics. In **engineering** or **macroscopic**
thermodynamics, on the other hand, the fluid is treated as a **continuum** with
measurable quantities such as pressure and temperature.

![Individual molecules (microscopic view). Engineering thermodynamics describes the gas as a whole instead, through properties such as $P$ and $T$.](figures/img/molecules-macro.png){width=26%}

## Thermodynamic terms and definitions

### System

A collection of matter enclosed within a prescribed boundary.

### Boundary

A surface, real or imaginary, that separates the system from its surroundings.
The boundary may be fixed, or it may be flexible and allow movement.

### Surroundings

Matter external to the system.

![Heat and work, and in some systems mass, can cross the boundary between the system and its surroundings.](figures/img/system-boundary.png){width=52%}

### Open, closed and isolated systems

**Open system** (also called a **control volume**): a system that freely
exchanges energy (work and heat) *and* matter with its surroundings.

**Closed system** (also called a **control mass**): a system where only work and
heat can cross the boundary. A closed system exchanges energy with its
surroundings, but not matter.

**Isolated system**: a system that exchanges neither matter nor energy with its
surroundings.

![](figures/out/system-types.svg){width=92%}

## Working fluid

The **working fluid** is the matter within the system boundaries, and it is
affected by any energy (heat and work) crossing the boundary. Common working
fluids are air, water, steam and refrigerants.

![Steam in a power station, air in a car engine, refrigerant in a fridge.](figures/img/working-fluids.png){width=62%}

### Phase

A **phase** is a quantity of matter with the same chemical composition that is
homogeneous throughout. Working fluids can exist in the solid, liquid or vapour
phase.

![](figures/img/phases.png){width=48%}

## State and property of a system

The condition of a system at any instant of time is called its **state**. The
**thermodynamic properties** of the fluid (for example $T$, $P$ and $V$) define
the state of a system. A property must be a characteristic that can be measured,
and it must have a unique numerical value when the fluid is in any particular
state.

The value of a property must be **independent of the process** through which
the fluid has passed in reaching that state.

![Temperature, pressure and volume of the gas can each be read off directly: they describe its state now, whatever happened to it before.](figures/img/state-properties.png){width=52%}

::: {.key}
It has been found experimentally that only **two independent properties** are
necessary and sufficient to determine the state of a closed system containing a
simple fluid.
:::

### Intensive vs extensive properties

Thermodynamic properties are divided into two general types, intensive and
extensive.

An **intensive** property is one that does *not* depend on the mass of the
system (for example $T$ and $P$). If we bring two systems together, intensive
properties are not summed.

An **extensive** property is one that *does* depend on the mass of the system
(for example $V$). If two systems are brought together, the extensive property
of the new system is the sum of the extensive properties of the original two
systems.

If we divide an extensive property by the mass, a **specific** property
results. For instance, the specific volume is defined as

::: {.key}
$$
v = \frac{V}{m}\;\left[\frac{\mathrm{m^3}}{\mathrm{kg}}\right]
  = \frac{1}{m/V} = \frac{1}{\rho}
$$
:::

::: {.note}
If an extensive property is represented by an **uppercase** letter, the
associated specific (intensive) property is denoted by a **lowercase** letter:
$x = X/m$.
:::

## Temperature

Temperature is a measure of molecular activity. In engineering thermodynamics,
however, the quantities of interest are defined in terms of macroscopic
observations only, so we proceed without defining temperature at the molecular
level.

### Thermal equilibrium

If there is no transfer of heat between two systems when they are brought into
thermal contact, they are said to be in **thermal equilibrium** with each other.
In this case, the temperatures of the two systems are the same: $T_1 = T_2$.

### Zeroth law of thermodynamics

::: {.key}
*"If two systems are in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in
thermal equilibrium with each other."*
:::

This law may seem so obvious that it does not need stating, but without it we
could not build thermometers.

![](figures/img/zeroth-law.png){width=40%}

A thermometer $C$ placed in contact with $A$ reads $T_C = T_A$; placed in
contact with $B$ it reads $T_C = T_B$. By the zeroth law, $A$ and $B$ are then
at the same temperature, $T_A = T_B$, without ever being brought into contact
themselves. That is exactly what we rely on every time we compare two
temperatures with a thermometer.

### Relative temperature scale (based on the zeroth law)

**Celsius** (or centigrade) is the most common temperature scale. The freezing
point of water is at $0~^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and its boiling point at
$100~^\circ\mathrm{C}$, with the interval between them divided into 100
degrees.

![Melting ice fixes 0 °C and boiling water 100 °C. Anders Celsius (Sweden, 1701–1744).](figures/img/celsius-scale.png){width=62%}

### Absolute temperature scale (based on the second law)

A definition of absolute temperature is possible with the second law of
thermodynamics (to be studied later). The **Kelvin** scale is the SI unit of
temperature, named after William Thomson, Lord Kelvin. A temperature in Celsius
is converted to kelvin as

::: {.key}
$$
T_\mathrm{K} = T_{^\circ\mathrm{C}} + 273.15
$$
:::

For example, $20~^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is $20 + 273.15 = 293.15~\mathrm{K}$.

![William Thomson, Lord Kelvin (UK, 1824–1907).](figures/img/kelvin.png){width=16%}

## Pressure

In gases and liquids, the effect of a normal force acting on an area is the
**pressure**. If a force $F$ acts at an angle to an area $A$, only the normal
component $F_n$ enters into the definition of pressure:

::: {.key}
$$
P = \frac{\Delta F_n}{\Delta A}
$$
:::

![](figures/img/pressure-surface.png){width=46%}

The pressure at a point in a fluid in equilibrium is the same in all directions:
it is a **scalar** quantity. The SI unit of pressure is the **pascal** (Pa),
where $1~\mathrm{Pa} = 1~\mathrm{N/m^2}$.

The pascal is a small unit, so pressure is usually given in kPa. Other common
units are the **bar** and the **atm**: $1~\text{bar}$ is exactly
$100\,000~\mathrm{Pa} = 100~\mathrm{kPa}$, and $1~\text{atm}$ is
$101\,325~\mathrm{Pa}$ ($1.01325$ bar), approximately the atmospheric pressure at
sea level.

### Absolute vs relative (gauge) pressure

Pressure as discussed above is called **absolute** pressure. Although absolute
pressure is what appears in most thermodynamic relations, pressure-measuring
devices often indicate the *difference* between the absolute pressure in a
system and the absolute pressure of the atmosphere outside the device. The
magnitude of this difference is called the **gauge** pressure.

::: {layout-ncol=2}
![](figures/img/tyre.png)

![](figures/img/tyre-gauge.png)
:::

::: {.key}
$$
P_\text{abs} = P_\text{gauge} + P_\text{atm},
\qquad P_\text{atm} \approx 101~\mathrm{kPa} \text{ at sea level}
$$
:::

::: {.note}
For a sense of scale: a diver 10 m under water feels roughly one extra
atmosphere, since $\rho g h \approx 1000 \times 9.81 \times 10 \approx
100~\mathrm{kPa}$.
:::

::: {.example}
The **gauge** pressure of a tank is 50 kPa. Calculate the **absolute**
pressure.

![](figures/img/gauge-absolute.png){width=36%}

*Hint: which relation links gauge and absolute pressure, and roughly what is the
atmospheric pressure?*

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="$P_\text{abs} = P_\text{gauge} + P_\text{atm}$, with $P_\text{atm} \approx 100$ kPa."}
$$
P_\text{abs} = P_\text{gauge} + P_\text{atm}
\approx 50~\mathrm{kPa} + 100~\mathrm{kPa} = \boxed{150~\mathrm{kPa}}
$$
:::
:::

::: {.example}
The piston has a mass of 10 kg and an area of $0.1~\mathrm{m^2}$. Find the
absolute pressure of the gas contained in the cylinder. Take
$P_\text{atm} = 100~\mathrm{kPa}$ and $g = 10~\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

![](figures/img/piston-10kg.png){width=22%}

**Step 1.** *The gas holds up the piston as well as the atmosphere above it.
What gauge pressure does the weight of the piston alone produce?*

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="$P_\text{gauge} = mg/A = 1000$ Pa $= 1$ kPa."}
$$
P_\text{gauge} = \frac{mg}{A}
= \frac{10~\mathrm{kg} \times 10~\mathrm{m/s^2}}{0.1~\mathrm{m^2}}
= 1000~\mathrm{Pa} = 1~\mathrm{kPa}
$$
:::

**Step 2.** *Now add the atmosphere.*

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="$P_\text{abs} = 1 + 100 = 101$ kPa."}
$$
P_\text{abs} = P_\text{gauge} + P_\text{atm}
= 1~\mathrm{kPa} + 100~\mathrm{kPa} = \boxed{101~\mathrm{kPa}}
$$
:::
:::

::: {.note}
In this course, the term *pressure* refers to **absolute pressure** unless
explicitly stated otherwise.
:::

### Pressure measurements

**Manometer.** The most basic device for measuring pressure is the manometer.
Manometers measure pressure differences in terms of the length of a column of
liquid such as water, mercury or oil. If one side of the manometer is open to
the atmosphere, the length of the liquid column gives the gauge pressure.

![](figures/img/manometer.png){width=40%}

Points $A$ and $B$ are at the same level in the manometer liquid. Above $B$ is a
column of liquid of height $H$, open to the atmosphere at the top.

::: {.gap height="20mm" hint="Pressure at $B$: the atmosphere plus the weight of the column over its area; $m = \rho A H$."}
$$
P_B = P_\text{atm} + \frac{mg}{A}
    = P_\text{atm} + \frac{\rho\,(A H)\,g}{A}
    = P_\text{atm} + \rho g H \tag{I}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="$A$ and $B$: same liquid, same level, at rest, so the same pressure. $A$ is at the fluid pressure $P$."}
$A$ and $B$ are in the same liquid, at rest, at the same level, so they are at
the same pressure; and $A$ is at the pressure $P$ of the fluid in the tank:
$$
P = P_A = P_B \tag{II}
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="10mm" hint="Combine (I) and (II)."}
Combining (I) and (II):
$$
P - P_\text{atm} = \rho g H
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
P_\text{gauge} = P - P_\text{atm} = \rho g H
$$
:::

**Barometer.** A barometer is a special manometer with one end closed above a
near vacuum ($P \approx 0$). Since there is almost zero pressure in the closed
tube above the column of liquid, the height of the column gives the atmospheric
pressure directly.

![](figures/img/barometer.png){width=26%}

::: {.gap height="14mm" hint="Above the column is (near) vacuum, so the pressure at $B$ is due to the column alone."}
Above the column there is (near) vacuum, so the pressure at the bottom of the
column, $B$, comes from the weight of the liquid alone:
$$
P_B = \rho g H_0
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="$A$ is at the free surface, open to the atmosphere; $P_A = P_B$ (same level)."}
$A$ is at the free surface, open to the atmosphere, and at the same level as $B$:
$$
P_A = P_\text{atm}, \qquad P_A = P_B
$$
:::

::: {.key}
$$
P_\text{atm} = \rho g H_0
$$
:::

::: {.example}
A mercury barometer located in a room has a height of 750 mm. What is the
atmospheric pressure in kPa? ($\rho_\text{mercury} = 13\,500~\mathrm{kg/m^3}$,
$g = 10~\mathrm{m/s^2}$)

*Hint: use the barometer relation we have just derived, with the height in
metres.*

::: {.gap height="16mm" hint="$P_\text{atm} = \rho g H_0 = 13500 \times 10 \times 0.75 = 101.25$ kPa."}
$$
P_\text{atm} = \rho g H_0
= 13\,500~\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m^3}} \times 10~\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s^2}}
  \times 0.75~\mathrm{m}
= 101\,250~\mathrm{Pa} = \boxed{101.25~\mathrm{kPa}}
$$
:::
:::

## Real fluid vs ideal fluid

As mentioned, two independent properties are necessary and sufficient to
determine the state of a system. To find the values of the other properties,
one can use **thermodynamic tables** for **real fluids**. These tables are
readily available in thermodynamics books.

![Part of a property table: once two properties (here $P$ and $T$) are fixed, the others can be read off.](figures/img/property-table.png){width=40%}

In thermodynamics and fluid mechanics we also often model fluids as **ideal**
(**perfect**) in order to approximate the behaviour of real fluids. An ideal
fluid is described by *mathematical equations*; a real fluid by *thermodynamic
tables*.

One of the best-known equations for ideal fluids is the **equation of state for
an ideal gas**. When a gas or a vapour has relatively low density, the following
equation is valid. A gas for which it is valid is called an **ideal gas**, or
sometimes a **perfect gas**:

::: {.key}
$$
PV = mRT
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P = \rho R T
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P v = R T
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Divide $PV = mRT$ by $V$: $m/V = \rho$."}
Dividing $PV = mRT$ by the volume, with $m/V = \rho$:
$$
P = \frac{m}{V}\,R T = \rho R T
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Divide $PV = mRT$ by $m$: $V/m = v$."}
Dividing $PV = mRT$ by the mass, with $V/m = v$:
$$
P\,\frac{V}{m} = P v = R T
$$
:::

where

| Symbol | Quantity | Unit |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $P$ | **absolute** pressure | Pa |
| $V$ | volume | m³ |
| $m$ | mass | kg |
| $R$ | gas constant | J/(kg K) |
| $T$ | temperature | **K** |
| $\rho$ | density ($= 1/v$) | kg/m³ |
| $v$ | specific volume | m³/kg |

| Gas | $R$ [J/(kg K)] |
|:--|--:|
| Air | 286.9 |
| Carbon dioxide (CO$_2$) | 188.9 |
| Helium (He) | 2077 |
| Hydrogen (H$_2$) | 4124 |
| Methane (CH$_4$) | 518.3 |
| Nitrogen (N$_2$) | 296.8 |
| Oxygen (O$_2$) | 259.8 |

: Individual gas constants.

::: {.warning}
When using the equation of state, pressure and temperature must be in **SI
units** and **absolute** quantities: absolute pressure, and temperature in
kelvin (K).
:::

Given that $Pv = RT$, for an ideal gas:

| | |
|:--|:--|
| $P \propto T$ | constant-volume process |
| $v \propto T$ | constant-pressure process |
| $P \propto 1/v$ | constant-temperature process |

![](figures/out/pv-ideal-processes.svg){width=62%}

::: {.note}
In microscopic and chemical studies, the equation of state is often written in
molar units, $PV = n R_0 T$, where $n$ is the number of moles (in kmol) and
$R_0$ is the **universal gas constant**, which has the same value for all ideal
gases: $R_0 = 8314~\mathrm{J/(kmol\,K)}$. One mole is about
$6.022 \times 10^{23}$ particles.

The two forms are linked through the **molar mass** $M$ of the gas, the mass of
one kmol in kg/kmol:

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="Both forms describe the same gas: $PV = mRT = nR_0T$, so $mR = nR_0$."}
Both forms describe the same gas, so
$$
PV = mRT = n R_0 T
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
m R = n R_0
$$
:::

::: {.gap height="12mm" hint="$m/n$ is the molar mass $M$, so $R_0 = MR$."}
and since $m/n$ is the molar mass $M$,
$$
R_0 = \frac{m}{n}\,R = M R
$$
:::

$$
R = \frac{R_0}{M}
$$
:::

::: {.note}
The value of $R$ is specific to each ideal gas, depending on its molar mass. For
oxygen, for example, $M = 32$ kg/kmol, giving
$R = 8314/32 = 259.8~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$, whereas $R_0$ has the same value for
all ideal gases.
:::

## End-of-chapter problems {#sec-ch1-problems}

::: {.tryfirst}
Have a real go at every problem here before you look at a solution. Worked
solutions are released after the lectures, but reading a solution is not the
same as being able to produce one: the time you spend stuck on a problem is
where most of the learning happens. Only once you have an answer of your own,
or have tried every approach you can think of, check it against the solution,
and compare the method, not just the final number.
:::

**P1.1 [easy].** Which of the following is **not** a property?

**(a)** heat &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** density &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** temperature
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** volume

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
**(a)** Heat is not a system property: it depends on the path followed during a
process, not only on the state of the system.
:::
:::

**P1.2 [easy].** Identify which of the following is an **intensive** property.

**(a)** a pressure of 90 kPa &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** a mass of 75 kg &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(c)** a 10 m³ volume &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 30 J of kinetic energy

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
**(a)** Pressure is independent of mass, so it is an intensive property. The
others would all double if, for example, the mass doubled.
:::
:::

**P1.3 [easy].** A 5 litre can of a particular brand of motor oil has a specific
volume of $0.0013~\mathrm{m^3/kg}$. Calculate its density.

**(a)** 769.2 kg/m³ &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 153.8 kg/m³ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(c)** 3846.0 kg/m³ &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 0.0325 kg/m³

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
Specific volume and density are
$$
v = \frac{V}{m}, \qquad \rho = \frac{m}{V}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\rho = \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{0.0013~\mathrm{m^3/kg}}
= \boxed{769.2~\mathrm{kg/m^3}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$

The 5 litres is not needed: density is an intensive property.
:::
:::

**P1.4 [easy].** A balloon contains $0.5~\mathrm{m^3}$ of air at a pressure of
1.02 bar and a temperature of 18 °C. What mass of air does the balloon contain?
(For air, $R = 287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$.)

**(a)** 0.61 kg &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 1.0 kg &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 0.00006 kg
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 9.9 kg

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
In SI units: $V = 0.5~\mathrm{m^3}$, $P = 1.02~\text{bar} = 1.02\times10^{5}$ Pa,
$T = 18~^\circ\mathrm{C} = 291~\mathrm{K}$.

For an ideal gas,
$$
PV = mRT
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
m = \frac{PV}{RT}
  = \frac{1.02\times10^{5}~\mathrm{Pa} \times 0.5~\mathrm{m^3}}
         {287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)} \times 291~\mathrm{K}}
  = \boxed{0.61~\mathrm{kg}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$
:::
:::

**P1.5 [easy].** Estimate the difference in density between the inside and the
outside of a house in winter, when $P = 100$ kPa,
$T_\text{inside} = 20$ °C and $T_\text{outside} = -20$ °C. For dry air,
$R = 287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$.

**(a)** 0.19 kg/m³ &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 0.17 kg/m³ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(c)** 0.15 kg/m³ &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 0.09 kg/m³

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
From the ideal-gas equation, $\rho = P/(RT)$, with the temperatures in kelvin:
$$
\rho_\text{out} = \frac{100\times10^{3}~\mathrm{Pa}}
                       {287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)} \times (-20 + 273)~\mathrm{K}}
               = 1.377~\mathrm{kg/m^3}
$$
$$
\rho_\text{in} = \frac{100\times10^{3}~\mathrm{Pa}}
                      {287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)} \times (20 + 273)~\mathrm{K}}
              = 1.189~\mathrm{kg/m^3}
$$
$$
\Delta\rho = 1.377 - 1.189 = \boxed{0.188~\mathrm{kg/m^3}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$
:::
:::

**P1.6 [medium].** Calculate the weight of a body that occupies $200~\mathrm{m^3}$
if its specific volume is $10~\mathrm{m^3/kg}$ ($g = 9.8~\mathrm{m/s^2}$).

**(a)** 196 N &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 20 N &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 132 N &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(d)** 92 N

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
From the specific volume,
$$
v = \frac{V}{m}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
m = \frac{V}{v} = \frac{200~\mathrm{m^3}}{10~\mathrm{m^3/kg}} = 20~\mathrm{kg}
$$
so the weight is
$$
W = m g = 20~\mathrm{kg} \times 9.8~\mathrm{m/s^2}
  = \boxed{196~\mathrm{N}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$
:::
:::

**P1.7 [medium].** The figure shows a tank within a tank, each containing air.
Pressure gauge A is located inside tank B and reads 1.4 bar. The U-tube manometer
connected to tank B contains mercury. Using the data on the diagram, determine
the absolute pressure inside tank A, in bar. The atmospheric pressure
surrounding tank B is 101 kPa, and $g = 9.81~\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

![](figures/img/p-tank-in-tank.png){width=62%}

**(a)** 2.68 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 3.54 &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 1.2 &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(d)** 0.4

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
Gauge A measures the pressure in tank A **relative to tank B**, not to the
atmosphere, so we first need the absolute pressure in tank B:
$$
P_{B,\text{abs}} = P_\text{atm} + P_{B,\text{gauge}} \tag{I}
$$

The manometer gives the gauge pressure of tank B, with
$\rho = 13.59~\mathrm{g/cm^3} = 13\,590~\mathrm{kg/m^3}$:
$$
P_{B,\text{gauge}} = \rho_\text{mercury}\, g L
= 13\,590 \times 9.81 \times 0.2 = 26.7~\mathrm{kPa} \tag{II}
$$

From (I) and (II):
$$
P_{B,\text{abs}} = 101 + 26.7 = 127.7~\mathrm{kPa} = 1.28~\text{bar}
$$

Now tank A:
$$
P_{A,\text{abs}} = P_{A,\text{gauge}} + P_{B,\text{abs}}
= 1.4~\text{bar} + 1.28~\text{bar} = \boxed{2.68~\text{bar}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$
:::
:::

**P1.8 [medium].** The gauge pressure reading on an automobile tyre is 240 kPa
when the tyre temperature is $-30$ °C. The automobile is driven to a warmer
climate, and the tyre temperature increases to 65 °C. Make reasonable
assumptions to estimate the gauge pressure of the tyre in the warmer climate.
The atmospheric pressure in both locations is 100 kPa.

**(a)** 333 kPa &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 473 kPa &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 373 kPa
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 260 kPa

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
**State 1:** $P_{1,\text{gauge}} = 240$ kPa, so
$P_{1,\text{abs}} = 240 + 100 = 340$ kPa; $T_1 = -30~^\circ\mathrm{C} = 243$ K.

**State 2:** $P_2 = ?$, $T_2 = 65~^\circ\mathrm{C} = 338$ K.

From the ideal-gas equation, $P/T = mR/V$. It is reasonable to assume that
neither the mass of air nor the volume of the tyre changes, so
$$
\frac{P_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{T_2}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
P_2 = 340~\mathrm{kPa} \times \frac{338~\mathrm{K}}{243~\mathrm{K}}
    = 472.9~\mathrm{kPa}
$$

This is absolute. The gauge reading is
$$
P_{2,\text{gauge}} = P_{2,\text{abs}} - P_\text{atm} = 473 - 100
= \boxed{373~\mathrm{kPa}} \quad \text{(c)}
$$

Always use **absolute** pressure in the ideal-gas equation. Using the gauge
readings directly gives 333 kPa, answer (a), which is wrong.
:::
:::

**P1.9 [medium].** A hollow metal sphere with an inside diameter of 150 mm is
weighed on a precision beam balance when evacuated, and again after being filled
to 875 kPa with an unknown ideal gas. The difference in mass is 0.0025 kg, and
the temperature is 25 °C. What is the gas? (*Hint: the volume of a sphere is
$\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, where $r$ is its radius.*)

| Gas | Formula | Molar mass (kg/kmol) | $R$ (kJ/(kg K)) |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| Steam | H$_2$O | 18.015 | 0.4615 |
| Acetylene | C$_2$H$_2$ | 26.038 | 0.3193 |
| Air | — | 28.97 | 0.287 |
| Ammonia | NH$_3$ | 17.031 | 0.4882 |
| Argon | Ar | 39.948 | 0.2081 |
| Butane | C$_4$H$_{10}$ | 58.124 | 0.1430 |
| Carbon dioxide | CO$_2$ | 44.01 | 0.1889 |
| Carbon monoxide | CO | 28.01 | 0.2968 |
| Ethane | C$_2$H$_6$ | 30.07 | 0.2765 |
| Ethanol | C$_2$H$_5$OH | 46.069 | 0.1805 |
| Ethylene | C$_2$H$_4$ | 28.054 | 0.2964 |
| Helium | He | 4.003 | 2.0771 |

**(a)** Helium &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** Air &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** Methanol
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** Ethane

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
The volume of the sphere:
$$
V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi \left(\frac{0.15~\mathrm{m}}{2}\right)^{3}
  = 0.00177~\mathrm{m^3}
$$

With $m = 0.0025$ kg, $T = 25~^\circ\mathrm{C} = 298$ K and
$P = 875\times10^{3}$ Pa, the ideal-gas equation gives the gas constant, which
has a specific value for each gas:
$$
PV = mRT
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
R = \frac{PV}{mT}
  = \frac{875\times10^{3}~\mathrm{Pa} \times 0.00177~\mathrm{m^3}}
         {0.0025~\mathrm{kg} \times 298~\mathrm{K}}
  \approx 2.08~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}
$$

According to the table, helium has the value of $R$ closest to this, so the gas
is **helium**, answer (a).
:::
:::

**P1.10 [medium].** Air in an internal-combustion engine is at 227 °C and
1000 kPa, with a volume of $0.1~\mathrm{m^3}$. Combustion heats it to 1500 K in
a constant-volume process. What is the mass of air, and how high does the
pressure become? ($R_\text{air} = 0.287~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$)

**(a)** 0.697 kg, 3000 kPa &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 0.345 kg, 4000 kPa &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(c)** 0.697 kg, 1000 kPa &nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 0.234 kg, 3000 kPa

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
With $T_1 = 227~^\circ\mathrm{C} = 500$ K, $P_1 = 10^{6}$ Pa and
$V_1 = 0.1~\mathrm{m^3}$, the ideal-gas equation gives the mass:
$$
m = \frac{P_1 V_1}{R T_1}
  = \frac{10^{6}~\mathrm{Pa} \times 0.1~\mathrm{m^3}}
         {287~\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)} \times 500~\mathrm{K}}
  = 0.697~\mathrm{kg}
$$

For the final state the volume does not change, $V_2 = V_1$:
$$
P_2 = \frac{m R T_2}{V_2}
    = \frac{0.697 \times 287 \times 1500}{0.1}
    \approx 3\times10^{6}~\mathrm{Pa} = 3000~\mathrm{kPa}
$$

Alternatively, since $m_1 = m_2$ and $V_1 = V_2$,
$$
\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \frac{T_2}{T_1}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
P_2 = 1000~\mathrm{kPa} \times \frac{1500~\mathrm{K}}{500~\mathrm{K}}
    = 3000~\mathrm{kPa}
$$

So the answer is **(a)**: 0.697 kg, 3000 kPa.
:::
:::

**P1.11 [hard].** Helium in a steel tank is at 250 kPa and 300 K, with a volume of
$0.1~\mathrm{m^3}$. It is used to fill a balloon. When the pressure drops to
150 kPa, the flow of helium stops by itself. If all the helium is still at
300 K, how big a balloon is produced? ($R_\text{helium} = 2.0771~\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$)

**(a)** 67 litres &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 93 litres &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 167 litres
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 7 litres

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
Take the system to be all of the helium: in the tank at first, in the tank plus
the balloon at the end. Its total mass and temperature are the same in the
initial and final states, so for an ideal gas
$$
P_1 V_1 = m R T = P_2 V_2
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
V_2 = \frac{P_1 V_1}{P_2}
    = \frac{250~\mathrm{kPa} \times 0.1~\mathrm{m^3}}{150~\mathrm{kPa}}
    = 0.167~\mathrm{m^3}
$$

The steel tank's volume does not change, so the difference between $V_2$ and
$V_1$ is the balloon:
$$
V_\text{balloon} = V_2 - V_1 = 0.167 - 0.1 = 0.067~\mathrm{m^3}
= \boxed{67~\text{litres}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$

$R$ is not needed.
:::
:::

**P1.12 [hard].** A glass is cleaned in hot water at 45 °C and placed on the table
bottom up. The room air at 20 °C that was trapped in the glass is heated up to
40 °C, and some of it leaks out, so that the net resulting pressure inside is
2 kPa above the ambient pressure of 101 kPa. Now the glass and the air inside
cool down to room temperature. What is the pressure inside the glass?
($P_\text{atm} = 101$ kPa)

**(a)** 96.4 kPa &nbsp;&nbsp; **(b)** 50.3 kPa &nbsp;&nbsp; **(c)** 115.4 kPa
&nbsp;&nbsp; **(d)** 167.8 kPa

::: {.gap height="fill"}
::: {.worked}
**While the air is hot** (after the leak):
$P_1 = P_\text{atm} + P_{1,\text{gauge}} = 101 + 2 = 103$ kPa,
$T_1 = 40~^\circ\mathrm{C} = 313$ K.

**After the air cools down:** $P_2 = ?$, $T_2 = 20~^\circ\mathrm{C} = 293$ K.

Once the glass sits sealed on the table, the mass and the volume of the trapped
air stay fixed. Assuming an ideal gas:
$$
P_1 V = m R T_1, \qquad P_2 V = m R T_2
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
P_2 = P_1 \frac{T_2}{T_1}
    = 103~\mathrm{kPa} \times \frac{293~\mathrm{K}}{313~\mathrm{K}}
    = \boxed{96.4~\mathrm{kPa}} \quad \text{(a)}
$$

$P_2 < P_\text{atm}$: there is a partial vacuum inside relative to the
atmosphere, so the atmosphere presses the glass against the table.
:::
:::
